title: Forward-50 Chase-Down Tackle
primarySkill: Completing a chase-down tackle inside attacking 50
objective: Develop the ability to chase an opponent exiting defensive 50, reach a safe side-on position and complete a legal tackle that creates a scoring opportunity.
groundSize: A lane approximately 25 metres long and 10 metres wide inside attacking 50.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position a defender with the football near the goal line or defensive pocket.
Place a chasing forward 3–5 metres behind and slightly inside.
Position an exit receiver near the end of the lane.
Place an attacking scoring target in front of goal.
A feeder or observer manages each repetition.
The ball carrier attempts to exit or dispose to the receiver.
The chaser must remain clear of direct contact through the opponent’s back.
Match players appropriately for speed and physical capacity.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier begins accelerating towards the exit receiver.
The chasing forward accelerates towards the opponent’s inside or outside hip.
The chaser attempts to close before the ball carrier reaches disposal range.
The defender may change pace once.
The chaser moves beside the ball carrier and decelerates.
A legal shoulder-and-wrap tackle is completed if safe range develops.
If the defender disposes, the chaser avoids late contact and continues towards the receiver.
The chaser scores two points for a tackle and one point for forcing an ineffective disposal.
If the forward wins possession, they have five seconds to attempt a score.
Rotate chaser, ball carrier, receiver and feeder roles.
coachingPoints: Sprint towards the ball carrier’s hip rather than directly at the spine.
Use the shortest legal pursuit angle.
Reduce the speed difference before contact.
Move beside the opponent before tackling.
Read the ball carrier’s disposal preparation.
Avoid contact after a clean kick or handball.
Continue pressure to the receiver if the disposal escapes.
Convert turnovers into a quick scoring attempt.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the chaser selects an effective angle.
Whether the defender’s speed is matched.
Whether contact occurs from the side.
Whether tackles remain above the knees and below the shoulders.
Whether late contact is avoided.
Whether the chaser continues to the next receiver.
Whether turnovers are converted into scoring opportunities.

commonErrors.error: Chaser runs directly into the opponent’s back.
commonErrors.correction: Pursue the hip and reach the side before contact.

commonErrors.error: Player reaches with one arm.
commonErrors.correction: Continue running until a two-arm wrap is available.

commonErrors.error: Tackler arrives at excessive speed.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and match pace.

commonErrors.error: Chaser makes contact after disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Pull out and continue pressure towards the receiver.

commonErrors.error: Player stops after forcing a poor disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Continue to the next contest.

commonErrors.error: Turnover is followed by a rushed shot.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and select the highest-value scoring option.

progressions: Add an overlap exit runner.
Allow the ball carrier unrestricted changes of pace.
Begin the chaser farther behind.
Continue into a two-versus-two forward-pressure contest.
Introduce match-like ground contact for prepared players.
regressions: Begin the chaser level with the opponent’s hip.
Reduce both players to jogging speed.
Use a moving tackle bag.
Replace the tackle with a pressure touch.
Predetermine the disposal point.
matchApplication: Forward chase-down tackles can create high-value turnovers close to goal. Successful forwards combine maximum running effort with enough control to avoid dangerous contact or late free kicks.
relatedDrills: TK-096 – Press Recovery After Kick Over the Top

title: Defensive Line Squeeze After Mark
primarySkill: Compressing defensive space after an opposition mark
objective: Teach a defensive unit to use the time created by an opposition mark to move forward, reduce receiver space and prepare coordinated pressure on the next possession.
groundSize: A grid approximately 35 metres long and 28 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position an attacking team across the grid.
Position defenders goalside and inside their direct opponents.
Begin with a controlled kick resulting in a mark.
Mark the protected area around the player who marks.
Place one central and two outside scoring gates.
The defender on the mark remains legal.
Other defenders use the pause to squeeze space and reorganise.
The marker may hold, kick or play on.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking player completes the mark.
The direct defender establishes the legal mark position.
Supporting defenders move forward and inside towards likely receivers.
Deeper defenders protect the long central target.
Players communicate opponent handovers created by the squeeze.
If the marker plays on, the direct defender applies immediate pressure.
If the marker disposes, the nearest defender closes the receiver while the football travels.
Legal tackles are permitted after possession is established.
Attackers score two points for a central exit and one point for an outside exit.
Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing a long uncontrolled kick.
Reset after each completed phase.
coachingPoints: Respect the protected area.
Use the mark to reset and compress defensive space.
Move forward together rather than individually.
Position inside likely receivers.
Protect the long central target.
Communicate handovers during the squeeze.
Remain ready for immediate play on.
Avoid squeezing so far that a long kick travels over the entire line.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender on the mark remains legal.
Whether supporting defenders squeeze immediately.
Whether likely receivers lose space.
Whether the long target remains protected.
Whether handovers are communicated.
Whether play-on pressure is immediate.
Whether the receiving player is pressured during the football’s flight.

commonErrors.error: Defenders stand still after the mark.
commonErrors.correction: Use the pause to reset and move forward.

commonErrors.error: Player on the mark enters the protected area.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the legal mark position until play on.

commonErrors.error: Defenders squeeze individually and create gaps.
commonErrors.correction: Move the entire line together.

commonErrors.error: Long central target becomes free.
commonErrors.correction: Keep a deeper defender protecting the dangerous space.

commonErrors.error: Players squeeze too close to short receivers.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain enough distance to react to a long disposal.

commonErrors.error: Defenders relax and concede play on.
commonErrors.correction: Stay balanced and ready for immediate movement.

progressions: Allow the marker to fake play on.
Add crossing receivers.
Increase kick distance.
Continue play for multiple possessions.
Introduce scoreboard and late-game scenarios.
regressions: Predetermine the next receiver.
Pause after the mark to position defenders.
Use handball only after the mark.
Replace tackling with pressure touches.
Reduce the number of receivers.
successIndicators: Respect the mark and protected area.
Squeeze space as a connected line.
Create pressure on the next possession.
matchApplication: An opposition mark gives defenders time to reorganise. Teams that squeeze forward together can remove easy receivers, force longer disposals and create tackle opportunities on the next possession.

title: Secondary Stoppage Pressure Chain
primarySkill: Maintaining pressure across repeated stoppages
objective: Develop the ability to rapidly reset defensive roles and maintain pressure through consecutive ball-ups or boundary stoppages.
groundSize: A stoppage area approximately 25 metres by 20 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Mark a central stoppage circle and four exit gates.
Position one ruck and two or three midfielders from each team.
A coach manages repeated ball-ups or throw-ins.
After each secondary stoppage, players have only five seconds to reset.
Full tackling begins after possession is established.
The drill continues for three to five consecutive stoppages before a full reset.
Rotate players through ruck, inside and outside roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins the first stoppage.
Players compete for possession.
Defenders pressure the first ball carrier and protect exit gates.
If a legal tackle creates a stoppage, the coach immediately prepares the next restart.
Players release, stand and reorganise within five seconds.
Direct opponents and likely receivers are reassigned.
The next stoppage begins.
The possession team scores one point for a clean exit.
The defending team scores one point for each forced secondary stoppage and two points for a turnover.
Continue for three to five stoppages.
Review whether pressure and structure improved or deteriorated through the chain.
coachingPoints: Release immediately once the stoppage is called.
Regain the feet and identify direct opponents.
Protect the most dangerous exit.
Communicate ruck, inside and outside responsibilities.
Pressure the first possession at every restart.
Avoid carrying frustration from one stoppage into the next.
Maintain legal tackle technique under repeated contact.
Be ready for changing tap and exit directions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players release promptly.
How quickly defensive roles are reset.
Whether opponents are identified.
Whether the same exit is repeatedly conceded.
Whether pressure remains strong across several stoppages.
Whether tackle technique deteriorates.
Whether communication improves after each restart.

commonErrors.error: Players remain on the ground after the stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Regain the feet immediately and reorganise.

commonErrors.error: Defenders lose direct opponents during the reset.
commonErrors.correction: Require visual or physical confirmation before the restart.

commonErrors.error: Players protect the previous exit pattern only.
commonErrors.correction: Read the new ruck and midfield setup.

commonErrors.error: Pressure declines after several stoppages.
commonErrors.correction: Rotate effort and maintain clear first-possession responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Tackles become high under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Lower through the hips or reduce the stoppage chain length.

commonErrors.error: Players argue about the previous contest.
commonErrors.correction: Reset attention to the next restart.

progressions: Reduce reset time to three seconds.
Change restart type between ball-up and boundary throw-in.
Add outside receivers.
Continue play after a clean exit.
Add scoreboard consequences for consecutive stoppage wins.
regressions: Reset fully after every stoppage.
Predetermine the tap direction.
Reduce player numbers.
Replace tackling with pressure touches.
Limit the chain to two stoppages.
successIndicators: Release and regain the feet quickly.
Improve organisation across the stoppage chain.
matchApplication: Matches often contain several stoppages in rapid succession. Teams must reset roles immediately and maintain pressure rather than losing structure or concentration after the first contest.

title: Boundary Throw-In Pressure Trap
primarySkill: Creating pressure from a boundary throw-in
objective: Develop coordinated pressure that prevents a clean boundary-stoppage exit and traps possession against the line.
groundSize: A boundary area approximately 25 metres long and 18 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use an existing boundary line or mark one side of the grid as the boundary.
Position two rucks and matched midfielders near the throw-in point.
Place outside receivers inside and behind the stoppage.
Mark a dangerous central exit gate and a lower-value boundary gate.
A coach performs controlled boundary throw-ins.
Defenders begin inside their direct opponents.
Full tackling begins once possession is established.
Rotate players through inside, outside and ruck roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach throws the football in from the boundary.
Rucks compete to direct the football.
Midfielders contest the first possession.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier.
Supporting defenders protect the central exit and likely handball receiver.
Defenders attempt to keep possession near the boundary.
Legal tackles may be completed once safe contact range develops.
The possession team scores two points for a central exit and one point for a boundary exit.
Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing another boundary stoppage.
If the football exits the immediate area, play continues for one disposal.
Reset and change the throw-in depth or player alignment.
coachingPoints: Protect the inside and central exit.
Position inside direct opponents.
Identify the likely first receiver.
The nearest balanced defender pressures the football.
Supporting defenders close the inside handball and backwards release.
Use the boundary as part of the defensive trap.
Avoid overcommitting into the ruck contest.
Maintain legal tackle height as players emerge.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders maintain inside position.
Whether central space is protected.
Whether the first ball carrier is pressured.
Whether likely receivers are covered.
Whether defenders keep the football near the boundary.
Whether tackles remain controlled in congestion.
Whether another stoppage is created.

commonErrors.error: Defenders stand boundary side of opponents.
commonErrors.correction: Reposition inside and protect the central exit.

commonErrors.error: Several defenders attack the ruck contest.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain outside and receiver coverage.

commonErrors.error: First possession escapes without pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the likely receiver before the throw-in.

commonErrors.error: Backwards handball remains available.
commonErrors.correction: Position a support defender behind the immediate contest.

commonErrors.error: Tackler arrives high from congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Lower through the hips and approach the torso.

commonErrors.error: Defenders force play inside rather than towards the line.
commonErrors.correction: Use body angle to maintain the boundary trap.

progressions: Allow unrestricted ruck plans.
Add a forward target beyond the stoppage.
Continue live play after the first exit.
Introduce late-game boundary scenarios.
Add a second consecutive throw-in after a forced stoppage.
regressions: Predetermine the tap direction.
Use a coach handball from the boundary.
Reduce player numbers.
Replace tackling with pressure touches.
Pause after the first possession.
successIndicators: Use the boundary to restrict space.
matchApplication: Boundary stoppages provide an opportunity to trap possession against the line. Strong inside positioning and first-possession pressure can prevent dangerous central clearances.

title: Intercept Turnover Counter-Pressure
primarySkill: Applying immediate counter-pressure after an intercept turnover
objective: Develop the immediate pressure response required when an attacking disposal is intercepted and the opposition begins a counterattack.
groundSize: Approximately half an oval with central and wide transition lanes.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position an attacking team moving towards goal.
Position one or two defenders in intercept positions.
Mark a central counterattack gate and two wide gates in the opposite direction.
The coach begins each repetition with an attacking entry.
The defending team attempts to intercept.
Once the intercept occurs, the original attackers must transition into counter-pressure.
Tackles remain controlled and legal.
Rotate intercept and attacking roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team moves the football towards goal.
A defender intercepts a kick or handball.
The original attacking team immediately becomes the pressure team.
The nearest balanced player closes the intercepting defender.
Other former attackers recover towards central counterattack lanes.
The intercepting team attempts to move the football through a transition gate.
Pressure responsibility rotates after each disposal.
Legal tackles are permitted once possession is established.
The intercepting team scores two points for a central exit and one point for a wide exit.
The counter-pressure team scores two points for winning the football back within eight seconds.
Continue until an exit, turnover or stoppage.
coachingPoints: React immediately when the intercept occurs.
Identify the interceptor as the new ball carrier.
The nearest balanced player applies direct pressure.
Recover through the corridor before searching for outside opponents.
Protect the first forward handball or kick.
Avoid emotional pauses after the attacking turnover.
Pressure the interceptor without conceding a high or late free kick.
Continue pressure across several disposals.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How quickly the attacking team recognises the turnover.
Whether the interceptor is pressured immediately.
Whether central counterattack lanes are protected.
Whether direct opponents are reassigned.
Whether pressure rotates after disposal.
Whether tackles remain controlled.
Whether the football is regained within the target time.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after the intercept.
commonErrors.correction: React immediately and identify the nearest pressure responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Every player runs directly towards the interceptor.
commonErrors.correction: Apply one pressure action and protect the counterattack options.

commonErrors.error: Defenders recover outside and concede the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Recover through central dangerous space first.

commonErrors.error: Tackler arrives recklessly because of frustration.
commonErrors.correction: Decelerate and maintain legal contact.

commonErrors.error: Pressure ends after the first disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Transfer responsibility to the next receiver.

commonErrors.error: Players remain focused on the failed attacking kick.
commonErrors.correction: Move attention immediately to the new possession phase.

progressions: Allow unrestricted full-field transition.
Add a scoreboard consequence for central exits.
Introduce several possible intercept locations.
Add a second intercepting defender.
Continue play after the counter-pressure turnover.
regressions: Predetermine the intercept player.
Pause briefly after the intercept.
Reduce transition distance.
Replace tackling with pressure touches.
Limit the intercepting team to handball.
successIndicators: Win back possession or force a slow exit.
matchApplication: Intercept turnovers can expose attacking teams defensively. Immediate counter-pressure can delay the opposition, prevent a clean rebound and create a second scoring opportunity.
relatedDrills: TK-096 – Press Recovery After Kick Over the Top

title: Pressure KPI Match Game
primarySkill: Applying measurable pressure behaviours in match play
objective: Develop and measure team pressure performance through a match-like game that rewards effective tackles, forced disposals, smothers, chase efforts and defensive role execution.
groundSize: Approximately three-quarters of an oval or full oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced match-positioned teams.
Use normal scoring in addition to a pressure scoreboard.
Assign coaches or non-playing players to record pressure actions.
Define the scoring system:
Two points for a legal tackle causing a turnover or stoppage.
One point for a tackle causing an ineffective disposal.
One point for a smother, chase or corral that changes the disposal.
One point for correctly denying the next receiver.
One bonus point for regaining possession within five seconds of a pressure action.
Contact is match-like for prepared players.
Play in three- to five-minute blocks.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins from a selected match restart.
Teams attempt to score normally.
Coaches record individual and team pressure actions.
The nearest balanced defender pressures the ball carrier.
Supporting defenders protect receivers and dangerous space.
Pressure scores are added separately from normal match scores.
A pressure action counts only when it clearly changes the opponent’s decision, disposal or movement.
Illegal, reckless or ineffective contact receives no pressure score.
At the end of each block, coaches provide one team-pressure statistic and one behavioural correction.
Teams restart from a different field position.
The winner may be determined by combined match and pressure scores.
coachingPoints: Reward effective pressure rather than uncontrolled effort.
A tackle should influence possession or disposal.
Corralling and receiver denial can be as valuable as direct contact.
Supporting defenders must protect the next option.
Pressure should remain connected across several possessions.
Legal technique is required for every scored action.
Players should react immediately after a pressure act.
Statistics should reinforce team behaviour rather than encourage individual chasing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether recorded pressure actions genuinely affect play.
Whether players chase individual statistics.
Whether supporting pressure is recognised.
Whether tackles remain legal.
Whether defenders transition after the first effort.
Whether pressure scores correlate with turnovers and field position.
Whether communication and structure improve across blocks.

commonErrors.error: Players chase the ball to collect pressure points.
commonErrors.correction: Reward receiver denial and structural pressure equally.

commonErrors.error: Soft contact is counted as an effective tackle.
commonErrors.correction: Score only actions that influence possession or disposal.

commonErrors.error: Players complete one pressure act and stop.
commonErrors.correction: Add value for repeat efforts and possession regain.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defenders receive no recognition.
commonErrors.correction: Record denied receivers and protected exits.

commonErrors.error: Tacklers become reckless to gain points.
commonErrors.correction: Remove scores for illegal or uncontrolled contact.

commonErrors.error: Coaches collect too many statistics to provide useful feedback.
commonErrors.correction: Select a small number of meaningful team KPIs.

progressions: Set team pressure targets for each block.
Compare pressure scores across field zones.
Add opponent-specific pressure objectives.
Use player-led KPI review.
Combine live observation with video analysis.
regressions: Track only tackles and forced turnovers.
Use controlled contact rather than match-like tackling.
Reduce game size and player numbers.
Pause after each pressure event to explain scoring.
Allocate one observer to each team.
successIndicators: Apply pressure that affects opposition play.
Understand pressure performance through measurable outcomes.
matchApplication: Pressure statistics are useful only when they reflect actions that change the opposition’s behaviour. Measuring tackles, forced disposals, receiver denial and repeat effort helps connect training standards with match performance.
relatedDrills: TK-080 – Team Pressure and Ball-Movement Assessment
TK-099 – Elite Chaos Pressure Match Simulation

title: Pressure Leadership and Tactical Assessment
primarySkill: Assessment of player-led tactical pressure
objective: Assess whether players can lead, organise and execute advanced pressure systems across tactical patterns, stoppages, transitions and match-like play.
groundSize: Full oval divided into five tactical assessment areas.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Construct five tactical assessment areas or phases.
Area 1 assesses player-led pressure organisation.
Area 2 assesses recognition of opposition exit patterns.
Area 3 assesses ruck-tap, boundary and secondary-stoppage pressure.
Area 4 assesses forward chase-down and intercept counter-pressure.
Area 5 assesses match-like pressure KPIs and leadership.
Nominate different leaders for each phase.
Assign coaches or observers to record performance.
Use one consistent scoring system across all areas.
Contact is match-like only for appropriately prepared players.
howTheDrillWorks:
In Area 1, a nominated player organises team pressure without coach assistance.
Observers assess scanning, communication, role allocation and adaptation.
In Area 2, defenders identify and counter repeated attacking exit patterns.
Observers assess recognition, anticipation and structural discipline.
In Area 3, players pressure first possession across ruck taps and repeated stoppages.
Observers assess reset speed, exit protection and tackle timing.
In Area 4, players complete forward chase-down and intercept counter-pressure scenarios.
Observers assess pursuit angles, turnover reaction and scoring conversion.
In Area 5, teams complete a pressure KPI match game.
Observers assess effective pressure actions, leadership and team connection.
Each assessed behaviour receives:
2 points: Demonstrated consistently and independently.
1 point: Demonstrated inconsistently or after prompting.
0 points: Not demonstrated or performed unsafely.
Any illegal or uncontrolled contact stops the repetition immediately.
Coaches record one technical strength, one tactical priority, one leadership priority and one recommended development drill for every player.
coachingPoints: Players should organise pressure independently.
Communication must identify specific roles and threats.
Opposition patterns should be recognised without reckless guessing.
First possession must be pressured at stoppages.
Repeated stoppages require rapid role reset.
Chase-down tackles must become side-on before contact.
Intercept turnovers require immediate counter-pressure.
Pressure KPIs should reflect genuine influence on play.
Legal tackling standards remain mandatory at match intensity.
Turnovers should create controlled attacking opportunities.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether leaders scan and communicate clearly.
Whether teammates respond to player-led calls.
Whether opposition patterns are recognised.
Whether defenders preserve structure while adjusting.
Whether stoppage pressure resets rapidly.
Whether chase-down tackles remain legal.
Whether counter-pressure follows intercepts.
Whether effective pressure actions are repeated.
Whether match context influences decisions.
Whether players require coach intervention.
Whether tackling remains safe under fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for coach instructions.
commonErrors.correction: Require nominated leaders to organise each phase.

commonErrors.error: Leadership calls are vague.
commonErrors.correction: Name the pressure player, receiver or space specifically.

commonErrors.error: Defenders guess opposition patterns too early.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm the cue before adjusting structure.

commonErrors.error: Stoppage roles are not reset.
commonErrors.correction: Release, regain feet and identify opponents immediately.

commonErrors.error: Chasers tackle directly through the back.
commonErrors.correction: Reach the hip and move beside the ball carrier.

commonErrors.error: Players pause after an intercept.
commonErrors.correction: Transition immediately into counter-pressure.

commonErrors.error: KPI scoring encourages individual chasing.
commonErrors.correction: Reward supporting pressure and receiver denial.

commonErrors.error: Tackle quality deteriorates under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce work duration and restore legal technique.

commonErrors.error: Turnovers are followed by rushed attacking decisions.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the first possession and select the best option.

progressions: Complete all five phases as one continuous full-ground simulation.
Remove nominated leaders and assess natural leadership.
Introduce opponent-specific tactical plans.
Add complex scoreboard and time scenarios.
Repeat under controlled match fatigue.
Use player-led review and KPI analysis.
regressions: Assess each area separately.
Provide leaders with role cards.
Predetermine attacking patterns.
Reduce contact from match-like to controlled.
Return players to TK-100 before repeating the complete assessment.
successIndicators: Preserve legal technique at match intensity.
matchApplication: Elite teams require players who can organise pressure, recognise opposition tactics and maintain safe tackling standards without constant coach direction. This assessment measures the transition from coached pressure systems to independent match execution.

title: Opposition Spare Counter-Pressure
primarySkill: Maintaining pressure against an opposition spare player
objective: Develop the ability to pressure the ball carrier while identifying and limiting the influence of an opposition spare without abandoning dangerous central space.
groundSize: A grid approximately 30 metres long and 24 metres wide with central and outside scoring gates.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Give the attacking team one additional player.
Mark one central scoring gate and two outside gates.
The spare attacker may move anywhere inside the grid.
Defenders begin in a connected shape protecting central space.
Nominate one defender as the pressure organiser.
The attacking team may use handball and short kicks.
Tackles remain controlled and legal.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession at one end.
The nearest balanced defender closes the ball carrier.
Supporting defenders identify direct opponents and the spare attacker.
Defenders protect the corridor and most dangerous receiver.
The pressure organiser communicates whether to hold shape, switch or leave the lowest-risk attacker.
The attacking team attempts to use the spare to progress through a scoring gate.
Defenders rotate pressure after every disposal.
A legal tackle may be completed when safe range develops.
Attackers score two points through the central gate and one point through an outside gate.
Defenders score two points for a tackle or turnover and one point for forcing three consecutive backwards or lateral disposals.
Reset after a score, turnover or stoppage.
coachingPoints: Accept that every attacker cannot be defended equally.
Protect the greatest scoring threat first.
The nearest balanced defender pressures the ball carrier.
Supporting defenders position between the football and dangerous receivers.
Leave the lowest-value option rather than opening the corridor.
Communicate who is responsible for the spare.
Move while the football is travelling.
Avoid charging at the spare and freeing a more dangerous player.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders identify the spare early.
Whether central space remains protected.
Whether the correct attacker is temporarily left free.
Whether direct pressure reaches the ball carrier.
Whether defenders communicate switches and handovers.
Whether the spare is forced into lower-value possession.
Whether tackle opportunities are created without structural collapse.

commonErrors.error: Defenders attempt to cover every attacker equally.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise the corridor, scoring gate and most dangerous receiver.

commonErrors.error: One defender chases the spare across the grid.
commonErrors.correction: Hold structure and hand responsibility over when appropriate.

commonErrors.error: Ball pressure disappears while players discuss the spare.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one active pressure defender at all times.

commonErrors.error: Defenders leave a central receiver free.
commonErrors.correction: Concede the widest or least dangerous option instead.

commonErrors.error: Pressure unit shifts too late.
commonErrors.correction: Move while the football is travelling.

commonErrors.error: Tackler lunges because of the numerical disadvantage.
commonErrors.correction: Corral and delay until a balanced tackle opportunity develops.

progressions: Give the attacking team two spare players.
Allow unrestricted kicking.
Remove the nominated pressure organiser.
Continue play after a turnover.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
regressions: Keep the spare player in one designated lane.
Predetermine the first two attacking disposals.
Use handball only.
Replace tackling with pressure touches.
Reduce the grid size.
matchApplication: Opposition teams often create a spare behind or around the football. Defenders must maintain pressure without destroying their structure by chasing every available player.

title: Tackle-to-Spread Transition
primarySkill: Transitioning from a completed tackle into attacking spread
objective: Develop the ability to convert a successful tackle or forced turnover into controlled attacking spread rather than remaining congested around the original contest.
groundSize: A grid approximately 24 metres long and 20 metres wide with four outside transition gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position two teams inside the central area.
Mark four coloured gates around the outside.
Begin each repetition with one team in possession.
A coach nominates the attacking direction after a turnover.
Legal tackles are permitted.
A turnover may be created through a tackle, spill, intercept or pressured disposal.
Once possession changes, the winning team must spread towards the called gate.
Play lasts a maximum of twelve seconds after the turnover.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins with possession in the central area.
The defending team applies connected pressure.
A defender completes a legal tackle or forces a turnover.
The tackler releases immediately.
The coach calls one coloured transition gate.
The team winning possession spreads away from the original contest.
The nearest player secures the loose football.
Teammates provide inside, outside and backwards support.
The new possession team attempts to move the football through the called gate.
The original possession team applies counter-pressure.
Two points are awarded for a tackle or turnover followed by a successful exit.
Reset after the exit, secondary turnover or stoppage.
coachingPoints: Complete and release the tackle before transitioning.
Identify when possession has genuinely changed.
The nearest player wins or secures the football.
Other players spread away from the tackle area.
Provide a safe first disposal.
Avoid every player gathering around the turnover.
Communicate the called exit gate.
Counter-pressure immediately if the first disposal is lost.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the tackler releases immediately.
Whether the football is secured before players spread.
Whether teammates create useful width and depth.
Whether the first disposal is controlled.
Whether congestion remains around the tackle.
Whether the opposition applies counter-pressure.
Whether the team maintains balance between spread and possession support.

commonErrors.error: Tackler remains attached after possession changes.
commonErrors.correction: Release immediately and become a support player.

commonErrors.error: Every player moves towards the loose football.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate one ball winner and spread the remaining players.

commonErrors.error: Team attacks before securing possession.
commonErrors.correction: Win the football first, then use the called exit.

commonErrors.error: First disposal is rushed into pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use the nearest clear support option.

commonErrors.error: Players spread too far and leave the ball winner isolated.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain short support before expanding fully.

commonErrors.error: Original attacking team stops after the turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Apply immediate counter-pressure.

progressions: Remove the coach-called gate and require players to identify the best exit.
Continue into a full scoring transition.
Add a second turnover during the phase.
Reduce the available transition time.
Use match-like contact for prepared players.
regressions: Predetermine the turnover and gate.
Pause after the tackle before beginning transition.
Use pressure touches instead of tackling.
Reduce player numbers.
Allow only handball after the turnover.
successIndicators: React immediately if possession is lost again.
matchApplication: Tackles create value only when the team can secure and use the resulting possession. Rapid spread after a turnover allows defenders to become attackers before the opposition reorganises.
relatedDrills: TK-029 – Tackle, Regain Feet and Rejoin

title: Three-Line Pressure Connection
primarySkill: Connecting pressure across defensive, midfield and forward lines
objective: Develop the connection required for pressure to transfer between team lines without leaving uncontested receivers or dangerous gaps.
groundSize: Full oval divided into forward, midfield and defensive thirds.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the oval into three horizontal thirds.
Position attackers and defenders in realistic match roles.
Begin the possession team in defensive 50.
Place one nominated pressure leader in each line.
Players may move between thirds as the football progresses.
Each defensive line must communicate when pressure responsibility transfers.
Use normal match disposal rules.
Match-like contact is used only for physically prepared players.
howTheDrillWorks:
The possession team attempts to move the football from defence to attack.
The forward line applies the first pressure on the defensive exit.
When possession enters the midfield third, the midfield leader calls the pressure handover.
Forwards recover behind the football and protect backwards options.
When possession enters the defensive third, defenders assume direct pressure responsibility.
Midfielders recover to protect the top of the defensive area.
The nearest balanced player in each line pressures the ball carrier.
Supporting players cover the next receiver and corridor space.
The possession team scores for reaching goal.
Defenders score for tackles, turnovers and forcing backwards transfers between thirds.
On a turnover, roles immediately reverse.
Play continues in blocks of three to five minutes.
coachingPoints: Pressure must transfer before the receiver gains time.
Each line should know when it becomes responsible.
Previous pressure players recover behind the football.
Protect central space during every handover.
Maintain one direct ball-pressure player.
Communicate receivers moving between lines.
Avoid multiple lines chasing the same possession.
Preserve tackle technique after long recovery runs.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether pressure handovers occur early.
Whether each line accepts responsibility.
Whether previous lines recover behind the football.
Whether receivers between lines are communicated.
Whether central gaps develop.
Whether tackle pressure arrives before the receiver accelerates.
Whether role reversal occurs immediately after turnovers.

commonErrors.error: Forwards continue chasing deep into midfield.
commonErrors.correction: Hand pressure over and recover behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Midfielders wait for the receiver to gain possession.
commonErrors.correction: Move during the football’s flight.

commonErrors.error: Defenders step up while midfield recovery is absent.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm connection before increasing pressure.

commonErrors.error: Players between lines become unmarked.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate receiver handovers early.

commonErrors.error: Several lines collapse on the football.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one pressure player and preserve structure behind.

commonErrors.error: Tackle technique deteriorates after long running.
commonErrors.correction: Decelerate and restore body position before contact.

progressions: Remove the zone lines.
Allow unrestricted switches.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
Require player leaders to organise without coach prompts.
Continue for longer match blocks.
regressions: Keep players within assigned thirds.
Predetermine the ball-movement route.
Use controlled contact instead of match-like tackling.
Pause at each pressure handover.
Reduce player numbers.
successIndicators: Complete legal tackles at match speed.
matchApplication: Full-ground pressure depends on connection between forwards, midfielders and defenders. If one line fails to accept or transfer responsibility, the opposition can move through uncontested space.

title: Opposition Tactical Adjustment Game
primarySkill: Adjusting pressure systems during live play
objective: Develop the ability to recognise when the opposition changes its ball-movement method and adjust the team’s pressure system without waiting for a coach stoppage.
groundSize: Approximately three-quarters of an oval or full oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two match-positioned teams.
Give the possession team several hidden tactical cards.
Tactical changes may include:
Short uncontested possession.
Long boundary kicking.
Corridor handball.
Repeated switches.
Use of a spare behind the football.
The defending team is not told when the attacking tactic changes.
Nominate defensive leaders in each line.
Match-like contact is used only for prepared players.
Coaches do not interrupt unless safety is compromised.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins with one attacking method.
The defending team applies its initial pressure structure.
At a designated moment, the attacking captain changes the tactic.
Defenders observe the changed movement pattern.
On-field leaders identify and communicate the adjustment.
The pressure team changes positioning, pressing triggers or receiver priorities.
Legal tackles continue throughout live play.
The attacking team scores normally.
Defenders receive two points for disrupting a tactical pattern within three possessions of identifying it.
Defenders receive one point for forcing the attack into a less dangerous pattern.
Play continues for three- to five-minute blocks.
Review whether the adjustment was identified early enough.
coachingPoints: Observe player positioning and disposal type, not just the football.
Communicate when the opposition pattern changes.
Adjust collectively rather than individually.
Preserve core principles of ball pressure and corridor protection.
Do not overreact to one unusual disposal.
Confirm the pattern across several cues.
Assign clear responsibilities after the adjustment.
Maintain legal tackling standards during tactical change.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How quickly players recognise tactical change.
Whether leaders communicate the adjustment.
Whether all three team lines respond.
Whether central space remains protected.
Whether the revised pressure system affects the opposition pattern.
Whether defenders overreact to isolated actions.
Whether tackle roles remain clear during restructuring.

commonErrors.error: Defenders continue the original plan despite repeated opposition success.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the changed pattern and adjust roles.

commonErrors.error: One player changes position without communicating.
commonErrors.correction: Make the adjustment a team call.

commonErrors.error: Defenders react to one disposal and lose structure.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm the pattern before making a major tactical change.

commonErrors.error: Tactical discussion causes ball pressure to disappear.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one immediate pressure player while leaders organise.

commonErrors.error: Players change everything at once.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust the smallest number of roles required.

commonErrors.error: Tackle discipline declines during confusion.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve approach control and legal contact standards.

progressions: Allow the opposition to change tactics multiple times.
Remove nominated leaders.
Add scoreboard and match-time scenarios.
Use opponent-specific tactical patterns.
Conduct player-led reviews between blocks.
regressions: Announce the tactical change.
Use only two possible attacking patterns.
Pause briefly after the change.
Use controlled contact instead of match-like tackling.
Reduce the playing area.
successIndicators: Maintain safe tackling during tactical change.
matchApplication: Opponents adjust during matches to escape pressure. Successful teams recognise those changes and respond on the field rather than waiting until the next quarter break.

title: Wet-Weather Tackle Pressure
primarySkill: Applying safe pressure in wet and slippery conditions
objective: Develop safe tackling and pressure behaviours when wet conditions reduce footing, ball control and the predictability of possession.
groundSize: A grid approximately 20 metres by 16 metres with one boundary side and two scoring gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Wet the footballs where conditions are dry.
Ensure the playing surface is safe and free from dangerous slipping areas.
Divide players into two small teams.
Mark one boundary side and two scoring gates.
Begin with a ground-ball or short-handball possession.
Players must remain upright during tackle contact.
Reduce running speed if footing becomes unsafe.
Stop immediately if the surface creates unacceptable injury risk.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach releases a wet football into the grid.
Players compete for possession.
The nearest defender applies controlled pressure.
Defenders use shorter approach steps to maintain footing.
Ball carriers may fumble or spill the football naturally.
Tacklers must release immediately if possession is lost.
Supporting defenders protect the likely ground-ball exit.
Teams score one point by moving the football through a gate.
Defenders score two points for a legal tackle or turnover and one point for forcing a boundary outcome.
Play continues for short blocks of 60–90 seconds.
Review footing, tackle height and spill reactions between blocks.
coachingPoints: Use shorter steps and a wider base.
Reduce closing speed earlier than in dry conditions.
Expect the football to spill or skid.
Keep the tackle target on the torso.
Avoid diving or sliding into the opponent’s legs.
Release immediately when possession is lost.
Use the boundary and body position to reduce movement options.
Prioritise safety if footing deteriorates.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players maintain footing.
Whether approach speed is adjusted.
Whether tackle height stays legal.
Whether players avoid sliding contact.
Whether tacklers release after spills.
Whether supporting defenders react to unpredictable football movement.
Whether the drill remains safe for the surface conditions.

commonErrors.error: Defender approaches with long uncontrolled strides.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the steps and lower the centre of gravity.

commonErrors.error: Player slides into the opponent’s legs.
commonErrors.correction: Stay upright and reduce speed earlier.

commonErrors.error: Tackler continues holding after a fumble.
commonErrors.correction: Release immediately and contest the loose football.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches the wet football and loses the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Track the torso and hips.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt dry-weather disposal and movement speed.
commonErrors.correction: Simplify decisions and control the pace.

commonErrors.error: Drill continues on an unsafe surface.
commonErrors.correction: Stop or modify the activity immediately.

progressions: Add repeated ground-ball contests.
Allow short kicks with a wet football.
Introduce boundary throw-in pressure.
Continue into a small-sided wet-weather game.
Add a time limit for disposal.
regressions: Use damp rather than fully wet footballs.
Reduce player numbers.
Use pressure touches instead of tackles.
Walk through approach footwork.
Remove competitive scoring.
successIndicators: Use simple and effective pressure decisions.
matchApplication: Wet football increases fumbles, ground contests and uncontrolled movement. Players must reduce approach speed, remain upright and react immediately when possession becomes loose.

title: Fatigue Decision Pressure Circuit
primarySkill: Maintaining pressure decisions under football-specific fatigue
objective: Assess and develop the ability to select the correct pressure action while physically fatigued without compromising legal tackling technique.
groundSize: Five stations occupying approximately one-third of an oval.
equipment: Heart-rate or work-time monitor where available
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Construct five connected stations:
Acceleration and deceleration.
Live corral-or-tackle decision.
Smother-or-tackle decision.
Recovery chase.
Two-player pressure rotation.
Players complete one action at each station before moving immediately to the next.
Work periods last 30–45 seconds.
Provide full recovery between sets.
Coaches monitor technique and stop unsafe repetitions.
Match players appropriately for contact stations.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin with a short acceleration and deceleration effort.
At Station 2, the attacker either enters tackle range or remains evasive.
The defender selects tackle or corral.
At Station 3, the ball carrier prepares to dispose or retains possession.
The defender selects smother pressure or a legal tackle.
At Station 4, the defender completes a recovery chase to a side-on pressure position.
At Station 5, two defenders rotate pressure against two attackers.
Coaches score each decision and technical action.
Players receive one point for the correct decision and one point for safe execution.
Any unsafe contact ends the player’s set.
Complete two to four sets per player.
coachingPoints: Fatigue does not justify poor tackle technique.
Decelerate before every contact decision.
Corral when safe tackle range is absent.
Smother when disposal is already committed.
Maintain legal tackle height.
Communicate during two-player pressure.
Stop the set if head position or body control deteriorates.
Prioritise quality over completion speed.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether decision accuracy declines under fatigue.
Whether deceleration becomes less effective.
Whether tackle height rises.
Whether players choose desperate contact.
Whether communication declines.
Whether recovery effort remains controlled.
Whether coaches intervene when safety standards fall.

commonErrors.error: Player treats every station as a tackle opportunity.
commonErrors.correction: Read the situation and select corral or smother when appropriate.

commonErrors.error: Deceleration disappears late in the set.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce speed earlier or end the repetition.

commonErrors.error: Tackler’s head moves in front of the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Restore side-on entry and reduce closing speed.

commonErrors.error: Player reaches because of fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Continue moving the feet or choose containment.

commonErrors.error: Communication stops at the final station.
commonErrors.correction: Require clear pressure and support calls.

commonErrors.error: Player prioritises circuit speed over safety.
commonErrors.correction: Score technical quality more heavily than completion time.

progressions: Reduce recovery between sets.
Randomise the station order.
Add scoreboard consequences.
Increase live attacking freedom.
Complete the circuit before a short match-simulation block.
regressions: Complete each station separately.
Reduce work periods.
Use tackle bags rather than live opponents.
Replace live tackles with pressure touches.
Predetermine the required pressure decision.
successIndicators: Make correct pressure decisions while fatigued.
Maintain safe tackle height and head position.
matchApplication: Late in quarters and during repeat contests, fatigue affects judgement as well as movement. Players must continue selecting the correct defensive action instead of relying on desperate tackle attempts.

title: Free-Kick Risk Pressure Management
primarySkill: Applying pressure without conceding avoidable free kicks
objective: Develop disciplined pressure that influences the opponent while avoiding high, low, late, in-the-back or protected-area infringements.
groundSize: A grid approximately 24 metres by 18 metres with four scenario zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the grid into four scenario zones:
Receiver after a mark.
Ball carrier preparing to dispose.
Ground-ball collector.
Boundary-side ball carrier.
Position attackers and defenders at each zone.
Coaches act as umpires and clearly signal outcomes.
Defenders score for effective legal pressure.
Attackers score for clean exits or free kicks.
Rotate players every three to four minutes.
Contact remains controlled.
howTheDrillWorks:
At the mark zone, the defender establishes a legal position and reacts to play on.
At the disposal zone, the defender pressures without making late contact.
At the ground-ball zone, the defender protects the player with their head over the football.
At the boundary zone, the defender corrals without driving the opponent over the line.
Coaches award two points for a legal tackle or turnover.
One point is awarded for pressure that forces a poor disposal.
The attacker receives two points for an avoidable defensive free kick.
Players must explain the pressure decision after selected repetitions.
Rotate through every scenario.
Finish with a short game in which free-kick discipline affects the score.
coachingPoints: Pressure is valuable only when it remains legal.
Respect marks and protected areas.
Avoid contact after clean disposal.
Protect the player whose head is over the football.
Move beside a rear-quarter opponent before tackling.
Corral near the boundary rather than driving through the player.
Release immediately when possession is lost.
Understand when not tackling is the best defensive decision.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players understand the different risk scenarios.
Whether approach speed is controlled.
Whether contact timing is legal.
Whether protected areas are respected.
Whether vulnerable players are protected.
Whether defenders choose containment when tackling is unsafe.
Whether repeated infringements reveal a technical or decision issue.

commonErrors.error: Defender contacts after disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the tackle action once the football is cleanly released.

commonErrors.error: Player enters the protected area.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the legal mark position until play on.

commonErrors.error: Tackler contacts a player over the football.
commonErrors.correction: Control the exit and wait until the player rises.

commonErrors.error: Defender drives directly through the back.
commonErrors.correction: Reach a side-on position before contact.

commonErrors.error: Tackler forces the opponent across the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the tackle and stop applying force.

commonErrors.error: Player believes pressure requires contact.
commonErrors.correction: Use corralling, smothering and receiver denial when tackling is unsafe.

progressions: Combine all scenarios in a continuous small-sided game.
Add scoreboard and red-time context.
Use player umpires to explain decisions.
Increase attacker freedom.
Apply match-like contact for prepared senior groups.
regressions: Walk through each scenario separately.
Use pressure touches rather than tackles.
Predetermine the correct defensive response.
Reduce movement speed.
Use coach demonstrations before live repetitions.
successIndicators: Avoid late, high, low and rear contact.
Select corral or smother actions when appropriate.
Maintain pressure without unnecessary free kicks.
Explain the reason for each decision.
matchApplication: Avoidable free kicks remove defensive pressure and give the opposition uncontested possession. Disciplined defenders influence play while recognising when contact is legal, unsafe or tactically unnecessary.

title: Match-Up Specific Tackle Planning
primarySkill: Adapting tackle strategy to different opponent types
objective: Develop individual tackle plans for opponents with different strengths, including speed, size, evasion, fend-off ability and preferred disposal side.
groundSize: Four contest lanes approximately 15 metres long and 8 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create four opponent profiles:
Fast straight-line runner.
Strong fend-off player.
Agile sidestep player.
Quick-disposal player.
Assign one attacker to perform each profile realistically.
Position one defender in each contest lane.
Give defenders time to identify a pressure plan before each repetition.
Rotate defenders through every opponent profile.
Match players appropriately for size and physical maturity.
All contact remains controlled.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defender reads the assigned opponent profile.
The defender states the intended pressure plan.
On the coach’s signal, the attacker enters the lane.
The fast runner attempts to use pace.
The fend-off player may use one controlled legal fend.
The agile player may use one or two direction changes.
The quick-disposal player attempts to release immediately.
The defender applies the planned approach, corral or tackle technique.
The defender receives one point for selecting an appropriate plan and one point for effective execution.
Players discuss whether the plan worked.
Rotate until every defender faces every profile.
coachingPoints: Adjust the approach to the opponent’s main strength.
Against speed, take an early pursuit angle and match pace.
Against a fend-off, maintain distance until the arm is committed.
Against agility, keep the feet active and protect dangerous space.
Against quick disposal, close while the football is travelling.
Avoid attempting the same tackle against every opponent.
Maintain legal tackle height and head position.
Revise the plan after each repetition.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders identify the opponent’s main threat.
Whether the pressure plan matches the profile.
Whether approach angles change appropriately.
Whether defenders remain disciplined against fends and fakes.
Whether quick-disposal players are pressured early.
Whether players revise ineffective plans.
Whether safety remains consistent across different match-ups.

commonErrors.error: Defender uses the same approach against every opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the specific threat and adjust distance, angle or timing.

commonErrors.error: Player races directly at the fast opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Take an interception angle and match speed.

commonErrors.error: Defender enters fend-off range too early.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain the buffer until the fend arm commits.

commonErrors.error: Player lunges at the agile opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Corral and keep adjustment steps active.

commonErrors.error: Defender reacts after the quick disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Close while the football is travelling or as possession is established.

commonErrors.error: Player changes technique so much that safety is lost.
commonErrors.correction: Adapt tactics without abandoning legal head and body position.

progressions: Hide the opponent profile until play begins.
Allow attackers to combine two strengths.
Add a support receiver.
Use opponent-specific match footage before the drill.
Continue into two-versus-two contests.
regressions: Announce the opponent’s intended movement.
Use one profile per session.
Reduce movement speed.
Replace tackling with pressure touches.
Allow coach-guided planning before each repetition.
successIndicators: Manage speed, fends, evasion and quick disposal.
matchApplication: Different opponents require different defensive approaches. Match-up planning helps players pressure an opponent’s weakness while reducing exposure to their preferred movement or disposal method.

title: Tackling and Pressure Match Rehearsal
primarySkill: Rehearsing complete tackling and pressure systems
objective: Rehearse all major individual and team-pressure behaviours in a structured match simulation before final chapter assessment.
groundSize: Full oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two match-positioned teams.
Play four scenario blocks:
Stoppage and first-possession pressure.
Defensive-50 exit and forward-half lock-in.
Turnover and counter-pressure.
Red-time full-ground press.
Nominate player leaders for each line.
Use normal AFL disposal and scoring rules.
Match-like contact is permitted only for appropriately prepared players.
Coaches observe without interrupting unless safety requires it.
Record pressure KPIs during each block.
howTheDrillWorks:
Block 1 begins from centre and boundary stoppages.
Teams are assessed on first-possession pressure and secondary stoppage response.
Block 2 begins with one team attempting to exit defensive 50.
The opposition applies a connected forward press.
Block 3 begins from an intercept, spill or coach-created turnover.
Both teams transition immediately into pressure or attack.
Block 4 begins with one team trailing late in the match.
The trailing team applies a full-ground press.
Coaches record tackles, forced disposals, receiver denial, recoveries and free-kick discipline.
Player leaders organise tactical adjustments.
Each block lasts five to eight minutes.
Complete a short player-led review between blocks.
coachingPoints: Apply safe individual technique within team structure.
The nearest balanced defender pressures the football.
Supporting defenders protect dangerous space and receivers.
Rotate pressure after every disposal.
Release and recover after tackles.
Protect vulnerable players at ground and aerial contests.
React immediately to turnovers.
Adapt pressure to scoreboard and tactical context.
Avoid preventable free kicks.
Use player leadership rather than constant coach instruction.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether tackle technique remains safe at match speed.
Whether pressure roles are clear.
Whether receivers and dangerous space are protected.
Whether stoppage exits are pressured.
Whether forward-half pressure remains connected.
Whether teams react immediately to turnovers.
Whether red-time decisions reflect match context.
Whether leaders organise adjustments.
Whether free-kick discipline is maintained.
Whether pressure KPIs reflect genuine influence.

commonErrors.error: Players chase individual tackles and lose team shape.
commonErrors.correction: Reward connected pressure and receiver denial.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defenders watch the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the next disposal option.

commonErrors.error: Tacklers remain at the completed contest.
commonErrors.correction: Release and recover into the next role.

commonErrors.error: Pressure disappears after turnovers.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the new ball carrier immediately.

commonErrors.error: Teams use the same pressure level in every scenario.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust according to field position, score and time.

commonErrors.error: Communication relies on coaches.
commonErrors.correction: Require player leaders to organise each block.

commonErrors.error: Match-like contact becomes uncontrolled.
commonErrors.correction: Stop play and return to controlled standards.

commonErrors.error: Pressure statistics reward ineffective contact.
commonErrors.correction: Count only actions that change possession, disposal or movement.

progressions: Remove the breaks between scenario blocks.
Allow captains to choose tactical adjustments.
Increase match duration.
Add opponent-specific patterns.
Complete the rehearsal under controlled match fatigue.
regressions: Complete each scenario separately.
Use controlled contact rather than match-like tackling.
Predetermine tactical responses.
Reduce player numbers and ground size.
Allow coaches to organise each restart.
successIndicators: Apply safe tackling at match speed.
Adapt to tactical and scoreboard scenarios.
matchApplication: This rehearsal combines the chapter’s technical, tactical and decision-making content into one match environment. It prepares players for final assessment and identifies any remaining individual or team-pressure weaknesses.
relatedDrills: TK-110 – Pressure Leadership and Tactical Assessment

title: Tackling and Pressure Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Final assessment of tackling and pressure capability
objective: Provide a complete chapter assessment of each player’s ability to execute safe tackles, make appropriate pressure decisions and contribute to coordinated team defence under match-like conditions.
groundSize: Full oval with six assessment zones and a final match-simulation area.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Construct six assessment zones:
Zone 1: Fundamental tackle technique.
Zone 2: Moving and evasive ball carriers.
Zone 3: Disposal, ground-ball and contest decisions.
Zone 4: Two- and three-player pressure.
Zone 5: Tactical team-pressure systems.
Zone 6: Match-scenario pressure and leadership.
Finish with a full-ground match simulation.
Assign qualified coaches or trained observers to every zone.
Match players appropriately for size, maturity and contact capacity.
Use controlled contact for developing players and match-like contact only for prepared senior players.
Apply the same scoring system at every zone.
Record individual technical, tactical, physical and communication outcomes.
howTheDrillWorks:
At Zone 1, players complete stationary, side-on and moving tackle entries.
Observers assess approach, head position, legal contact height, wrapping, control and release.
At Zone 2, defenders face live evasion, changes of pace, rear-quarter pursuit and fend-off situations.
Observers assess balance, patience, recovery and tackle timing.
At Zone 3, players select between tackle, corral and smother around disposal, ground-ball and aerial-contest situations.
Observers assess decision quality, opponent protection and free-kick discipline.
At Zone 4, defenders complete two-versus-two and three-player pressure activities.
Observers assess role allocation, receiver denial, communication and tackle support.
At Zone 5, teams complete stoppage, corridor, boundary and forward-half pressure scenarios.
Observers assess structure, pressure rotation and tactical execution.
At Zone 6, players manage scoreboard, fatigue, chaos and opposition tactical adjustments.
Observers assess leadership, match awareness and adaptability.
Each behaviour receives:
- 3 points: Consistently demonstrated independently at match standard.
- 2 points: Consistently demonstrated under controlled conditions.
- 1 point: Demonstrated inconsistently or after correction.
- 0 points: Not demonstrated or performed unsafely.
Any illegal, reckless or uncontrolled contact stops the repetition immediately.
Players complete a final match simulation in which chapter behaviours are observed without regular coach intervention.
Coaches produce an individual tackling-and-pressure development profile for every player.
coachingPoints: Safety is the first and non-negotiable assessment standard.
Contact must remain below the shoulders and above the knees.
Head placement must remain beside or behind the opponent.
No sling, lifting, rotation or unnecessary ground force is permitted.
Players must decelerate before contact.
Defenders should recognise when to tackle, corral, smother or delay.
Vulnerable ground-ball and aerial-contest players must be protected.
Tacklers must release promptly.
Players must recover into the next defensive action.
Team pressure requires one ball defender and connected support.
Central and dangerous space should be protected.
Communication and leadership must continue under fatigue.
Match context should influence risk.
Preventable free kicks reduce the assessment result.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Acceleration and deceleration into contact.
Near-foot placement.
Legal tackle height.
Safe head position.
Two-arm wrapping.
Upright control and prompt release.
Response to evasion, pace and fend-offs.
Recovery after missed or broken tackles.
Decision making around disposal.
Protection of players over the football.
Smother and corral selection.
Receiver denial and defensive support.
Pressure rotation after disposals.
Corridor and boundary positioning.
Stoppage and turnover reaction.
Tactical adjustment.
Communication and leadership.
Technique under fatigue.
Free-kick discipline.
Transition after winning possession.

commonErrors.error: Player approaches contact without decelerating.
commonErrors.correction: Restore the final short adjustment steps before reassessment.

commonErrors.error: Head position moves in front of the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Return to side-on entry and reduce approach speed.

commonErrors.error: Tackler contacts high or below the knees.
commonErrors.correction: Rebuild legal torso targeting under controlled conditions.

commonErrors.error: Player reaches instead of completing a two-arm wrap.
commonErrors.correction: Continue foot movement until close enough to secure the body.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts tackles from unsafe rear positions.
commonErrors.correction: Reach the hip line and move beside the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Player tackles when corral or smother is required.
commonErrors.correction: Reassess the possession and disposal cues before committing.

commonErrors.error: Tackler fails to release after a spill or whistle.
commonErrors.correction: Make release behaviour part of every repetition.

commonErrors.error: Player stops after the first pressure action.
commonErrors.correction: Add recovery and next-action scoring.

commonErrors.error: Several defenders chase the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate one pressure player and protect receivers with others.

commonErrors.error: Team concedes central space while pressing.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise the corridor and greatest scoring threat.

commonErrors.error: Communication declines under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce work duration and require consistent role calls.

commonErrors.error: Match urgency creates illegal contact.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain technical standards regardless of score or time.

commonErrors.error: Turnover possession is used recklessly.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the first disposal and create attacking spread.

progressions: Complete the assessment at full match intensity.
Add opponent-specific tactical patterns.
Use video review for individual tackle technique.
Compare pressure KPIs with match data.
Repeat selected zones under controlled fatigue.
Allow player leaders to conduct the final review.
Develop position-specific assessment standards.
Reassess identified weaknesses after a targeted training block.
regressions: Assess technical zones separately.
Reduce contact from match-like to controlled.
Use tackle bags before live opponents.
Replace tackling with pressure touches where required.
Predetermine attacking movements and decisions.
Reduce player numbers and field size.
Return players to the relevant earlier chapter drills before reassessment.
successIndicators: Use safe head and shoulder placement.
Select tackle, corral, smother or delay appropriately.
Adapt to tactical and match scenarios.
Convert pressure into possession and controlled attack.
matchApplication: The final assessment determines whether players can transfer isolated tackling technique into safe, intelligent and coordinated match pressure. Successful players combine physical execution with decision making, communication, tactical awareness, discipline and repeat effort.
relatedDrills: TK-060 – Pressure and Contest Block Assessment
TK-080 – Team Pressure and Ball-Movement Assessment
TK-110 – Pressure Leadership and Tactical Assessment
